passage_text: Researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of a novel antihypertensive drug in reducing systolic blood pressure (SBP) among adults with stage‑1 hypertension. Four hundred participants were enrolled and stratified into four age groups: 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, and 60–69 years. Baseline SBP values were recorded, followed by a 12‑week treatment period during which the drug was administered daily. Post‑treatment SBP was measured at week 12. The results, summarized in Table 1, show that all age groups experienced a reduction in SBP. The magnitude of the reduction varied across age groups, with younger participants showing a slightly higher percentage decline. Baseline SBP increased with age, but the absolute reduction in SBP was remarkably similar across the groups, ranging from 18 to 20 mmHg. These findings suggest that the drug’s antihypertensive effect is consistent across age ranges, though the relative benefit appears greater in younger adults.
stem: Which age group experienced the greatest percent reduction in systolic blood pressure?
explanation: Percent reduction = (Baseline – Post)/Baseline × 100. For 30–39 it is (150 – 130)/150 = 13.3%, the largest among all groups (11.4%, 12.1%, and 11.8% for the others).
trap: Absolute reductions are nearly identical (18–20 mmHg), so comparing mmHg alone would not separate the groups; the denominator (baseline) matters.

stem: Which study design would best determine whether the drug’s effect differs by age group?

options.A: Randomized controlled trial with age‑stratified randomization
options.D: Prospective cohort study without age stratification

explanation: A randomized controlled trial that stratifies participants by age ensures balanced allocation within each age group and allows direct comparison of drug effects across ages.
trap: Choosing an observational design because it seems closer to real-world practice; only randomization with stratification balances confounders within each age group.

stem: What is the simple (unweighted) average of the four group percent reductions in systolic blood pressure?
explanation: Correct: A) The mean of 13.3, 11.4, 12.1 and 11.8 is 12.15%, which rounds to 12.2%. Why the others are wrong: B) 12.5% does not follow from the four percentages. C) 13.0% is close to the single 30-39 value (13.3%) rather than the mean. D) 13.5% is above the highest single-group value (13.3%), so it cannot be a mean of these four.
trap: Averaging the absolute reductions or using the 30-39 value of 13.3% alone; the question asks for the mean of the four percentages (about 12.15%).

stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.A: The drug reduces SBP in all age groups.
options.B: The percent reduction is highest in the 30-39 group.
options.C: The absolute reduction is higher in older patients.
options.D: The baseline SBP is higher in older patients.

explanation: Correct: C) Absolute reductions are 20, 18, 20 and 20 mmHg for the four groups in age order, so there is no increase with age. Why the others are wrong: A) Every group fell from baseline to post-treatment, so this is supported. B) The 30-39 group has the largest percent reduction (13.3%), so this is supported. D) Baseline SBP rises from 150 to 170 mmHg with age, so this is supported.
trap: Because older patients start with higher SBP, it is tempting to assume they also lose more mmHg; the absolute drops (20, 18, 20, 20) show no age trend.

stem: Which explanation best accounts for the observed trend in percent reduction?

options.A: Age‑related vascular stiffness increases drug efficacy.
options.B: Younger patients metabolize the drug faster.
options.C: Older patients have higher baseline SBP, but absolute reductions are similar, so the same mmHg drop is a smaller percentage.
options.D: The drug is more potent in younger patients.

explanation: Baseline SBP rises with age (150 to 170 mmHg) while absolute reductions stay about 18–20 mmHg, so the percent reduction is slightly lower in older groups.
trap: Attributing the trend to age-related drug potency or metabolism; the passage gives no mechanistic data, only that similar mmHg drops from higher baselines are smaller percentages.
